blocks.content: You finished your design and feel relieved. Then the interviewer smiles and says, "now what if we add this?" The follow up phase is where the interview is often truly won or lost.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974123487-311860597.png

Follow up questions are not attacks. They are the interviewer checking whether your design can grow, and whether you can think on your feet. A design that extends cleanly is the strongest signal you can give.
This lesson covers why follow ups come, the common types, and exactly how to handle each with a calm, structured approach.

blocks.title: The mindset to hold
blocks.content: Treat every follow up as a chance to show your design breathing and growing, not as a hole being poked. Curiosity beats defensiveness.
1. Why Interviewers Ask Follow Ups
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972247564-51244756.png
blocks.alt: Follow ups test flexibility, calm, and communication

blocks.content: The extension phase reveals things a first pass design simply cannot.

["Whether your design is flexible or brittle when requirements change.","Whether you can reason calmly under a little pressure.","Whether your earlier principles were real or just decoration.","How you communicate tradeoffs when there is no perfect answer."]
items: Whether your design is flexible or brittle when requirements change.
Whether you can reason calmly under a little pressure.
Whether your earlier principles were real or just decoration.
How you communicate tradeoffs when there is no perfect answer.

blocks.content: The Common Types of Follow Up
blocks.text: The Common Types of Follow Up

blocks.content: Most follow ups fall into a few familiar buckets. Recognising the type helps you respond with confidence.

{"headers":["Type","Example"],"rows":[["New feature","Now support electric vehicle charging spots"],["New variation","Add a new pricing model"],["Scale change","What if there are many parking lots in a city?"],["Edge case","What happens if a ticket is lost?"],["Tradeoff probe","Why did you choose this over that?"]]}
When a follow up lands, silently label which type it is. That single step turns a scary question into a familiar one.
2. Extend, Do Not Rewrite
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972249182-288786588.png
blocks.alt: Add a new class, do not rewrite the design

blocks.content: The best answer to "add a new type" is usually to add a new class, not to edit your existing ones. This is the Open Closed principle finally paying off.

blocks.title: Why this lands well
blocks.text: If your design lets you answer a follow up by adding one small class, the interviewer sees your structure was genuinely clean. That is the whole payoff of the earlier steps.

blocks.content: Think Out Loud
When a follow up lands, do not go silent and freeze. Narrate your thinking so the interviewer can follow and even help.

blocks.title: A calm script
blocks.content: Try: "Good question. This is a new variation, so I would add it as a new class implementing the same interface, which means my existing classes stay untouched." That one sentence shows structured thinking.
3. New Feature Follow Ups
A new feature asks the system to do something it did not before, like electric charging spots. Add the new entity and connect it, without disturbing what works.

codes.python:
class ElectricSpot(Spot):
    def start_charging(self): ...   # new behaviour, existing spots unaffected

blocks.content: Because Spot was a clean base, a new kind of spot slots in as a subclass, and the parking logic that works with spots keeps working.
New Variation Follow Ups
A new variation is a different version of something you already have, like another pricing rule or payment method. If you used a Strategy, this is trivial.

codes.python:
class CryptoPayment(Payment):
    def pay(self, amount): ...      # just another strategy

blocks.content: One new class implementing the existing interface, and you are done. This is exactly why choosing the Strategy pattern earlier pays off now.
4. Scale Follow Ups
Some follow ups push on scale, like handling many parking lots across a city. You do not need a full distributed system, just show your classes can be organised to grow.
Introduce a higher level class that manages the collection, and explain how responsibilities stay separated even as the system gets bigger.
Edge Case Follow Ups
Edge cases probe the unusual situations, like a lost ticket or a full lot. Handle them by deciding the rule and putting it in the right place.
["A lost ticket: charge a flat penalty, handled in the pricing service.","A full lot: reject at the gate with a clear message.","An invalid vehicle: refuse entry before issuing a ticket."]
items: A lost ticket: charge a flat penalty, handled in the pricing service.
A full lot: reject at the gate with a clear message.
An invalid vehicle: refuse entry before issuing a ticket.

blocks.content: Edge cases show you think about the real world, not just the happy path. Naming a few before being asked is a strong move.
5. Tradeoff Probes
Sometimes the interviewer asks why you chose one design over another. They are not attacking, they want your reasoning.
Answer honestly with the tradeoff. "I used composition here instead of inheritance because the relationship is not a true is a, and composition stays more flexible if the requirements change."
There is rarely one perfect answer in design. Showing you understand the tradeoff is worth more than defending a single choice.
Staying Calm Under Pressure
The follow up phase can feel like the interviewer is poking holes. They are, but with good intent. Here is a simple routine to stay composed.

["Pause and restate the question in your own words.","Name the type of change it is, a new variation, a scale change, an edge case.","Explain where in your design it fits and why.","Make the change in code, or describe it clearly if time is short."]
items: Pause and restate the question in your own words.
Name the type of change it is, a new variation, a scale change, an edge case.
Explain where in your design it fits and why.
Make the change in code, or describe it clearly if time is short.

blocks.content: This routine turns any surprise into the same four calm steps, so you never freeze.
6. A Worked Follow Up Walkthrough
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782973104503-946879132.png
blocks.alt: An electric spot is added as a subclass of Spot

blocks.content: Let us run a real one end to end on the parking lot.

blocks.title: The follow up
blocks.text: Interviewer: now the lot should support electric vehicles that need charging while parked. How does your design handle it?

blocks.content: You named the change, added one class, and explained the small tweak to spot finding. The rest of the design never moved. That is a clean extension, and it is exactly what earns the strong score.
7. When a Follow Up Breaks Your Design
blocks.text: 7. When a Follow Up Breaks Your Design

blocks.content: Sometimes a follow up genuinely does not fit your current design. Do not panic or pretend. Recognising the weakness out loud is itself a strong signal.

Say what would need to change and why, then make the adjustment. "My current design assumed one gate. To support many, I would pull gate handling into its own class so the lot is not tied to a single entry."

blocks.title: Honesty scores
blocks.content: Admitting a limitation and describing the fix shows maturity. Interviewers trust candidates who can see their own design clearly.
8. The First Ten Seconds of a Follow Up
blocks.text: 8. The First Ten Seconds of a Follow Up

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972252415-488695827.png
blocks.alt: The calm four step routine for any follow up

blocks.content: How you react in the first moments sets the tone. Do not blurt out code. Take a breath, restate the question, and name its type. This buys thinking time and shows composure.
A short, calm pause to understand the question is far stronger than a fast, panicked answer that misses the point.
9. Anticipating Follow Ups While You Design
blocks.text: 9. Anticipating Follow Ups While You Design

blocks.content: The best defence is a clean design built with change in mind. As you design the first version, quietly ask what the interviewer is likely to add, and keep those doors open.
["New types? Put them behind an interface so new classes slot in","New rules? Isolate them in their own class or strategy","More of something? Make sure a manager class could hold many"]
items: New types? Put them behind an interface so new classes slot in
New rules? Isolate them in their own class or strategy
More of something? Make sure a manager class could hold many

blocks.title: Design for the question you expect
blocks.content: You cannot predict every follow up, but pricing rules, new item types, and scale are asked so often that leaving room for them is almost free.
10. A Second Walkthrough: Monthly Passes
Another common follow up on the parking lot: support monthly pass holders who park for free.
Because pricing was a strategy, a monthly pass becomes one new pricing class plus a check for whether the driver holds a pass. The core design barely moves.
11. Turning a Follow Up Into a Discussion
blocks.text: 11. Turning a Follow Up Into a Discussion

blocks.content: Strong candidates treat follow ups as a two way conversation, not a quiz. Offer a choice and its tradeoff, and invite the interviewer in.

For example: "I could handle this with a new subclass, or with a strategy. The strategy is more flexible if more variations are coming. Which direction do you expect this to grow?" This shows senior thinking.
12. Ending the Interview Strong
When the follow ups wind down, briefly summarise your design and how it handled the changes. A confident wrap up leaves a strong final impression.
["Recap the core classes and their responsibilities","Note how the design absorbed each follow up cleanly","Mention one improvement you would make with more time"]
items: Recap the core classes and their responsibilities
Note how the design absorbed each follow up cleanly
Mention one improvement you would make with more time

blocks.content: Finish by showing your design grew gracefully. That final image, of a clean design bending to new needs, is what the interviewer remembers.
13. Follow Ups Are a Good Sign
blocks.text: 13. Follow Ups Are a Good Sign

blocks.content: Remember that reaching the follow up phase usually means your core design was solid enough to build on. Interviewers extend designs they respect. Treat the questions as a sign you are doing well, not a warning that you are failing.
A stream of follow ups is often the sound of an interview going right. Stay calm, stay curious, and keep extending.
14. Common Mistakes

{"pros":["Extend by adding new classes","Narrate your reasoning out loud","Stay calm and curious","Admit tradeoffs and limits honestly"],"cons":["Rewriting your whole design in a panic","Going silent while you think","Getting defensive about your choices","Pretending there is one perfect answer"]}
15. Common Questions
What if a follow up breaks my whole design? - Stay calm and say so honestly, then describe how you would adjust. Recognising the weakness is itself a strong signal.
Do I have to fully code every follow up? - No. Often explaining clearly where the change fits and why is enough, especially when time is short.
How do I prepare for follow ups? - Design cleanly from the start. A design built on single responsibility and open closed almost always extends gracefully.
What if I do not know the answer? - Reason out loud toward a sensible one. You are judged on your thinking, not on having every answer ready.

blocks.content: Handle follow ups with a clean, extendable design and a calm, spoken thought process, and you will finish the interview strong. That completes the full LLD interview approach, from the first clarifying question to the last extension.
